questions.question: Define rejuvenation and explain the two main families of causes, using the correct terminology for each.
questions.expected_answer: Rejuvenation is when a river regains erosive energy and resumes vigorous vertical erosion because its relationship with base level — the lowest level to which it can erode, ultimately sea level — has changed. The two main causes are a drop in base level, called eustatic change when sea level falls, for example during an ice age; and uplift of the land through tectonic or isostatic movement, which steepens the river's gradient. Increased discharge, for instance after river capture, is a supporting cause. The knickpoint where the new steeper profile meets the old one retreats upstream.

questions.question: Name and explain the four landscape features produced by rejuvenation, with a South African example for at least one.
questions.expected_answer: The knickpoint — a sharp break of slope in the long profile, usually a waterfall or rapids retreating upstream, as at Augrabies Falls on the Gariep. Paired river terraces — remnants of the old floodplain stranded as matching flat benches on both valley sides when the river cut down through its own floor; repeated rejuvenation builds a staircase, oldest at the top. Valley-in-a-valley — the cross-sectional form of a young steep-sided valley incised into the floor of the old broad valley. Incised meanders — the river's loops cut vertically into rock, entrenched when symmetric from fast downcutting, ingrown when asymmetric, as in the winding Blyde River canyon.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of river capture and identify the five features of a capture landscape, stating one consequence for the captor and one for the victim.
questions.expected_answer: A stronger river — steeper gradient, softer rock or higher rainfall — extends its source backward by headward erosion through the watershed until it intersects a neighbouring river's channel, and the neighbour's headwaters divert into the steeper, lower course. Features: the captor stream, the captured stream, the elbow of capture where the flow makes an unnatural sharp bend, the misfit stream — the beheaded lower course too small for its broad valley — and the wind gap, the abandoned dry valley through the high ground. The captor's increased discharge boosts its energy and often causes rejuvenation; the victim's lower course is starved of water, affecting downstream users, and its valley may silt up.
